inputs.question: When an operator submits an invalid edit at the approval pause, why doesn't the approval step just keep prompting in a loop until the edit is valid?

gold.quote: Forbidden by LangGraph's index-based resume matching; a second resume could be served the first value

reference_outputs.reference_answer: LangGraph matches resume values to interrupt() calls by index within one node execution, so looping interrupt() inside the node could serve a later resume the earlier value. Instead the node interrupts once, records the validation error in a control field, and a conditional edge routes back to the approval node to ask again.

inputs.question: Why does the investigation router pick evidence sources with a keyword table instead of asking the model which sources to read?

gold.quote: Ask the model which sources to query | The router would no longer be deterministic, and the evidence-sufficiency evaluator could not be deterministic either

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Letting the model choose sources would make the router non-deterministic, and then the evidence-sufficiency evaluator could not be deterministic either. A keyword table in code keeps routing deterministic given the state and readable by anyone who wants to change it.

inputs.question: Why does the live model smoke test run from its own workflow file rather than as an extra manually-triggered job in the main CI workflow?

gold.quote: The file would contain `secrets.`; the existing test's one-job and no-secrets assertions would have to be weakened, and the keyless proof becomes a conditional instead of a byte-level fact

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Putting the job in the main CI file would mean that file references secrets, weakening the test that asserts it has exactly one job and no secrets. A separate dispatch-only file keeps the main CI file byte-identical, so 'the default job reads no secret' stays provable.

inputs.question: Why was the incident graph built as an explicit state graph instead of using an agent framework like Deep Agents with human-in-the-loop middleware?

gold.quote: The point is a fixed approval gate, typed control fields and deterministic routing; Deep Agents lets the model plan its own steps, which is the baseline, not the design

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The project's point is a fixed approval gate, typed control fields and deterministic routing. Deep Agents lets the model plan its own steps, which is what the comparison baseline does, not the design being built.

inputs.question: Why did the team cut the number of human approval points down to Design and Ship?

gold.quote:
five checkpoints the human had nothing to decide at
(every approval note on the client-style app was "none")

human waited 41, 10 and 17 hours on runs whose agents worked 7 hours, 3 hours 40 minutes and
1 hour 45 minutes

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Timestamps from three real changes showed the human was waiting far longer than agents worked (41, 10 and 17 hours of waiting), and several checkpoints had nothing to decide, with approval notes reading 'none'. So the pipeline was reduced to two human touches (Design and Ship), plus Deploy at tier 3.

inputs.question: When the ECC plugin was evaluated, why didn't the team swap WorkHorse's own agents out for ECC's?

gold.quote:
Replacing WorkHorse's agents was rejected: ECC's agents do not write gate packets, do not use
`wh.js`, and do not produce the artifacts Paddock watches.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: ECC's agents don't write gate packets, don't use wh.js and don't produce the artifacts Paddock watches, so swapping them in would remove the governance part specific to WorkHorse and keep only the generic part. WorkHorse instead vendored the parts of ECC that improve its agents and kept its own orchestration.

inputs.question: Why was the smallest risk tier's agent-time budget raised from 15 minutes?

gold.quote:
The tier 0 budget of 15 agent-minutes was not reachable: a verify pass and a review pass with
their fixes cost about 25 minutes on a one-file change, and that rigour is the product.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Fifteen agent-minutes was not reachable: a verify pass plus a review pass with fixes took about 25 minutes even on a one-file change, and that rigour is the product. The tier 0 budget became 25 minutes from 0.3.6.

inputs.question: Why does the hybrid retrieval use a reciprocal rank fusion constant of 10 rather than the usual 60?

gold.quote: ranking, so the textbook k=60 (tuned on far larger corpora) mostly just adds tail noise here.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: In the dev tuning loop k=10 beat k=30 and k=60 on recall, MRR and precision. A smaller k concentrates weight on results already near the top of a ranking, which suits a corpus of about 600 chunks, while the textbook k=60 was tuned for far larger corpora and mostly adds tail noise here.

inputs.question: Did splitting a question into sub-questions help answer questions that span two documents, and why was that approach dropped?

gold.quote: **It over-splits.** 13 of 34 questions were split, most of them single-document
Tuning the prompt against seven cross-doc questions would be fitting dev, not fixing retrieval.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: No: decomposition lowered coverage (27/34 to 23/34 overall, 3/7 to 2/7 on cross-doc). It over-split single-document questions, its guard blocked the splits that mattered, and even correct splits lost, so it was rejected; tuning the prompt on seven questions would have been fitting the dev set.

inputs.question: Why won't the question-answering service start without an API key instead of just running unauthenticated?

gold.quote:
rather than falling back
to no auth -- a failure that is silent and consequential is the one shape the security baseline
forbids.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The corpus holds client-shaped material and named people, so the data routes are never served open. Falling back to no auth would be a silent, consequential failure, which the security baseline forbids, so the server refuses to start without a key of at least 32 characters.

inputs.question: Why doesn't the portfolio use hash-based URLs to avoid the GitHub Pages deep-link problem?

gold.quote: Produces URLs that look broken on a resume and that some applicant-tracking systems mangle, which is the exact audience this site exists for

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Hash URLs like /Portfolio/#/work/... look broken on a resume and some applicant-tracking systems mangle them, and recruiters are exactly the audience the site exists for.

inputs.question: Why are the site's typefaces bundled with the site rather than loaded from Google Fonts?

gold.quote: Leaves an unsettled legal question open forever and keeps a third party on every page view, to save four dependencies. Rejected by the owner at G1

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Using Google Fonts would keep a third party on every page view and leave the GDPR lawful-basis question permanently unsettled, just to save a few dependencies; the owner rejected it. Self-hosting via fontsource packages means no third party sees visitors and the font versions are pinned and updated like other dependencies.

inputs.question: Why are the GitHub Actions in the deploy workflow pinned to commit hashes instead of version tags like v5?

gold.quote: A tag is mutable: whoever controls the action can move `v5` to new code that runs with `id-token: write` in this repository. The SHA removes that

reference_outputs.reference_answer: A tag is mutable, so whoever controls an action could move it to new code that would run with the deploy job's id-token write permission. Pinning to a full commit SHA removes that risk, and Dependabot keeps the SHAs current.

inputs.question: A static site with no logins or user input arguably doesn't need a Content Security Policy, so why does the portfolio ship one?

gold.quote: Rejected because the tag costs one build step and "no CSP" is a due-diligence question with an embarrassing answer on an engineering portfolio

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Going without a CSP was considered defensible, but it was rejected because the policy costs only one build step and 'no CSP' would be an embarrassing due-diligence answer on an engineering portfolio. It is injected at build time only, so the dev server is unaffected.

inputs.question: How close do the top two root-cause scores have to be before the incident graph treats the diagnosis as ambiguous and escalates?

gold.quote:
`is_ambiguous` returns true when `root_cause` is null or when
the two highest re-scored scores differ by less than `AMBIGUITY_MARGIN = 0.15`

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The run is ambiguous when the root cause is null or when the two highest re-scored hypothesis scores differ by less than 0.15 (AMBIGUITY_MARGIN); ambiguous output goes to escalate.

inputs.question: How is the investigation budget for evidence reads calculated?

gold.quote: Budget is derived: `12 - (number of source read attempts recorded in actions)`, clamped at 0

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The budget is derived as 12 minus the number of source read attempts recorded in the actions list, clamped at 0 by merge. Later the router reserves both read attempts per source so total reads can never exceed 12.

inputs.question: What is the minimum number of passing tests the incident-response project's CI requires before the job counts as green?

gold.quote:
fails the job
when passed tests (tests minus skipped, failures and errors) are below 30

reference_outputs.reference_answer: 30. A script reads the JUnit report and fails the job when passed tests (excluding skipped, failed and errored ones) fall below 30.

inputs.question: What agent-time budget does each WorkHorse risk tier get?

gold.quote:
Budget
for tier 0 is 25 minutes from 0.3.6; tiers 1 to 3 stay at 30, 90 and 180.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Tier 0 gets 25 agent-minutes (raised from 15 in 0.3.6), tier 1 gets 30, tier 2 gets 90 and tier 3 gets 180; a profile's budgets.agent_minutes can override these.

inputs.question: How many builder agents can run in parallel during the build phase?

gold.quote:
dispatches one `wh-builder` per task in the wave, all at once, up to `build.max_parallel` from
the profile (default 10, hard-capped at 10)

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Up to build.max_parallel builders per wave, which defaults to 10 and is hard-capped at 10; each runs in its own isolated worktree on its own task branch.

inputs.question: Which model generates the cited answers, and how many model calls does it make per question?

gold.quote:
Haiku 4.5 (`claude-haiku-4-5`, the plan's default), one call per question, no
tools

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5) generates the answers, with one call per question and no tools.

inputs.question: What made vector queries ignore the HNSW index and fall back to a sequential scan?

gold.quote: `retrieve/hybrid.py`'s `retrieve_vector` -- ordered by `<->`, the **L2** operator. pgvector only

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The index was built with vector_cosine_ops but queries ordered by the L2 operator <->, and pgvector only uses an index whose opclass matches the ORDER BY operator. Switching to the cosine operator <=> fixed it, cutting p50 latency on 100k vectors from about 21.5 s to 55.5 ms with identical results.

inputs.question: Which Node release line does the portfolio repository tell developers and CI to use?

gold.quote: `.nvmrc` contains the single line `22`. It names the release line developers and CI should use;

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The Node 22 release line. The exact 22.12.0 floor is enforced separately through the engines field with engine-strict.

inputs.question: Which typeface families does the redesigned portfolio use?

gold.quote:
`package.json` adds `@fontsource/ibm-plex-sans` 5.3.0 and
`@fontsource/ibm-plex-mono` 5.3.0, keeps `@fontsource/space-grotesk` (bumped to 5.3.0 so the
three families share one release)

reference_outputs.reference_answer: IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono and Space Grotesk, all self-hosted through fontsource packages at 5.3.0; Inter and JetBrains Mono were removed.

inputs.question: What did the last release of the desktop app change compared with the one before it?

gold.quote:
Bundles WorkHorse 0.3.10 instead of 0.3.1. 0.5.0's bundled copy predated the fixes that let a
  headless run edit a sensitive path its approved Design names (0.3.4)

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Paddock 0.5.1 only updated the bundled plugin from WorkHorse 0.3.1 to 0.3.10, with no app code changes. The older bundled copy lacked fixes such as letting a headless run edit a sensitive path its approved Design names, so runs stopped in Build.

inputs.question: How does a human approval work in AgentOps compared with WorkHorse?

gold.quote:
WorkHorse enforces gates with hooks on every tool call and files on disk. AgentOps enforces
them with a typed state graph and a checkpointer.

They approve, reject with a reason (the
graph goes back to investigate with that reason in its next prompt) or edit the remediation

This is the human act in the loop. The command records who (from `git config user.email`),
when, the tier, and your notes.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: AgentOps pauses the graph with LangGraph's interrupt() and the operator approves, rejects with a reason, or edits the remediation, all enforced by a typed state graph and checkpointer. WorkHorse enforces its gates with hooks on every tool call and files on disk: the human runs the approve command, which records who, when, the tier and notes in a committed approvals file.

inputs.question: How is the Studbook search that runs inside the desktop app kept equivalent to the reference Python implementation?

gold.quote:
retrieval reproduces this repo's published numbers to four
places, and the ported parser and chunker produce byte-identical ids and hashes

reference_outputs.reference_answer: Through parity gates: a Node port of the query path was compared question by question with the Python pipeline, and retrieval must reproduce the published recall, MRR and precision to four places with byte-identical parser and chunker output. Paddock's dependency upgrades, such as transformers.js 4.3.0, were held to those same gates.

inputs.question: How do AgentOps and Studbook each stop their held-out evaluation split from being used for tuning?

gold.quote:
`tests/test_dataset.py` recomputes every line and fails on any difference, so any
edit to a held-out scenario, or to the manifest, is a deliberate, reviewed change to an ask-first
file.

`--split test` requires typing "yes" at a prompt, on purpose: the held-out split is scored once,
  not touched during tuning

reference_outputs.reference_answer: AgentOps pins its held-out scenarios with a manifest and committed sha256 checksums that a test recomputes, so any edit is a deliberate reviewed change. Studbook makes scoring the test split require typing 'yes' at a prompt, because the held-out split is scored once and not touched during tuning.

inputs.question: The portfolio first served deep links through a copied 404 page; why was that later changed to writing a real page per route?

gold.quote:
the HTTP status on every path except `/` is 404. Search
engines will not index `/work` or any `/work/:slug` page
The 404 status is exactly what breaks previews, which is the request

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The original approach copied index.html to 404.html, so deep links worked but returned HTTP 404, which was accepted for human visitors. Link previews broke because of that 404 status, so the build began writing a directory index.html copy for each defined route, returning 200 while keeping 404.html for unknown paths.

inputs.question: Which human approvals did a tier 2 change need under the original WorkHorse design, and which does it need now?

gold.quote: | 2 | schema, auth, payments, PII, infra, third-party integration | G1, G2, G3, G4, G5 |
Required gates by tier: 0 → G4; 1 and 2 → G2, G4; 3 → G2, G4, G5.

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The original design required all five gates (G1 to G5) for tier 2. Since the two-gates redesign, tier 2 needs only G2 (Design) and G4 (Ship), with the security reviewer still mandatory and rollback rehearsed.

inputs.question: How did the Gate screen's approve action change between the original desktop app design and the two-gates release?

gold.quote:
Approve: a notes field and a button labelled with the gate. Reject: the same with notes
  required.

Every decision starts on its recommendation, so the primary action reads "Approve as
  recommended" until an override is picked

reference_outputs.reference_answer: The original design had an Approve button labelled with the gate plus a notes field, and Reject with required notes. From Paddock 0.5.0 every decision starts on its recommendation, so the primary action reads 'Approve as recommended' until an override is picked, and the other action is 'Reject with notes'.
